opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it comes down to a simple observation: the world is far bigger and messier than anything we can hand-design for. If I build an agent and give it a fixed model of its world, I've baked in my assumptions, and those assumptions are almost always going to be wrong in some way, especially once the agent is out there interacting with real people in real situations.

A lot of my work has been with prosthetic limbs and assistive devices. The person wearing the device, the way they move, how their muscles fatigue over a day, how they change over months, how sweaty the socket gets, none of that is something I can write down ahead of time. The only way the system can really keep up is to learn continually from its own stream of experience: the sensor signals, the actions it takes, what happens next.

Prediction is the core of that. If an agent can learn to anticipate what's coming, like what a signal will look like in half a second, or whether the user is about to switch from the elbow to the hand, it starts to build up knowledge that's grounded in its own experience. We've thought about this in terms of general value functions: lots of predictive questions an agent asks and answers about its sensorimotor stream, learned online and in real time. Those predictions become a kind of model of the world that's checkable and verifiable by the agent itself. It can see whether it was right and correct itself, without a human in the loop labeling everything.

That matters for scalability, too. Learning from raw experience means the agent's knowledge can grow as its experience grows, rather than being capped by what a designer could anticipate. And in a partnership setting, between a person and a machine, it means the machine is actually adapting to that specific person, not some average idea of a person. That's where I think the real power is: agents that keep learning, keep predicting, and become better partners the longer you work with them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predicting future sensor signals and learning from raw experience, but does not say predictions operate on raw bits rather than human-defined numerical variables.

r002.rationale: The response says fixed, hand-designed models may encode wrong assumptions, but does not identify human ways of segmenting the world as the limitation on interaction with diverse environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that I want agents that can keep learning on their own, in the world, for as long as they're operating. And if that's your goal, you pretty quickly run into the question of what the agent should actually be learning. My answer, and this really comes out of the reinforcement learning tradition at Alberta, is predictions. Lots of them. Predictions about what the agent's own sensors are going to say next, predictions about what will happen if it takes some particular action, predictions about how long until something changes.

The reason I like predictions grounded in raw experience is that they come with their own supervision. The agent makes a forecast, time passes, and the world tells it whether it was right. There's no human in the loop labeling things, no separate dataset. So the agent can just keep checking itself against reality, every moment, forever. That's a really powerful property. It means the knowledge the agent has is always being tested and refined by what it's actually experiencing, rather than being frozen at whatever we handed it at design time.

And once you have a rich set of those predictions, interesting things start to happen. The predictions themselves become a kind of representation. An agent that knows "if I push here, I'll feel resistance in about half a second" or "this signal tends to go up when that one goes down" has, in a very practical sense, a model of its world. Not a big symbolic map, but something built up from the actual stream of sensation and action. And you can use those predictions as features for learning other things, including how to act well.

A lot of my own work has been with people using prosthetic limbs, and that's where this really hit home for me. Every person is different, every day is a bit different, the device gets bumped, the muscle signals drift. If the system can only do what we programmed it to do in the lab, it falls apart. But if it's constantly predicting what the user is about to do and what the sensors are about to report, and updating those predictions from experience, it can adapt alongside the person. It becomes a partner rather than a tool.

So I'd say it comes down to this. Experience is the one thing an agent always has. If we build systems that can turn that experience into verifiable predictive knowledge, we get agents that can grow with the world instead of being left behind by it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predictions grounded in raw experience and sensor signals, but does not say agents predict incoming experience at the level of raw bits rather than human-defined numerical variables.

r002.rationale: The response mentions adapting to variation in users, days, devices, and sensor signals, but does not explain that structuring agents around human ways of segmenting the world can limit interaction with diverse environments.

astra-6.text:
Because prediction gives an agent a way to turn experience into something useful. It’s not just sensing what’s happening right now; it’s learning what to expect next, including how its own actions affect those expectations. That’s a foundation for making better decisions.

If we specify everything in advance, we’re limited by what we, as designers, anticipated. An agent that learns from its interactions has the opportunity to adapt to the particular environment it’s in and to keep adapting as that environment changes.

And those predictions can be grounded in things the agent can actually check: Did the signal arrive? Did the movement have the expected result? That connection between expectation and experience is very powerful. It gives the agent a continual way to improve its understanding, rather than relying entirely on an understanding we handed it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prediction from raw experience and signals, but does not say agents predict incoming experience at the level of raw bits rather than human-defined numerical variables.

r002.rationale: It says pre-specifying everything can limit adaptation, but does not connect that limitation to structuring agents around human ways of segmenting the world or to diverse environments.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an agent’s experience is ultimately what it has to work with. We can give it a model of the world, but that model reflects our assumptions about what matters, and those assumptions may not hold when the agent encounters something new.

If it can learn predictions directly from its own interaction with the world, it can continually ask: What do I expect to happen next? How will that change if I take this action? And then it can check those expectations against what actually happens. That gives it a way to adapt and to ground its knowledge in things it can observe and test.

For me, that’s particularly compelling when you think about a system working closely with a person. The person changes, the environment changes, and the relationship between them changes. You want the system to keep learning from that shared experience, rather than depend entirely on what a designer anticipated beforehand.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning predictions from interaction, but does not specify prediction at the level of raw bits rather than human-defined numerical variables.

r002.rationale: It says designer assumptions may not hold in new situations, but does not clearly connect human ways of segmenting the world to limits on interacting with diverse environments.
